title: Victims can't sue SIU for negligence
subtitle: Simone Wellington alleges a slipshod investigation by the SIU has prevented her from understanding the circumstances surrounding the shooting death of her son, Duane.
article: Victims and their families have no right to sue the province's Special Investigations Unit for negligent investigations of crimes committed by police officers, the Ontario Court of Appeal has ruled.

The SIU's role in investigating cases of death or serious injury involving police is geared toward protecting the public at large, not answering to particular victims and their families, the court said Friday.
"In my view, the SIU does not and should not conduct criminal investigations to advance the private interest of any individual citizen," Justice Robert Sharpe wrote on behalf of a three-judge panel.

The court was ruling in a case brought forward by the mother and sister of 15-year-old Duane Christian, who was killed by police while he was at the wheel of a stolen van in the parking lot of his Scarborough apartment building on June 20, 2006.
The appeal court was told the SIU failed to interview the officer who fired the fatal shot and closed its investigation before receiving a pathologist's report.

As a result of Friday's decision, victims are prevented from suing not just the SIU, but any police force for negligence, argues Julian Falconer, a lawyer representing Aboriginal Legal Services of Toronto, which intervened in the case.
"Now families are simply out of luck," he said, "in the face of incompetence by any investigative body."
However, the law permits police officers targeted by the SIU to sue for negligent investigations, even though victims and their families can't, Falconer said.
Sharpe addressed that issue in Friday's decision.
There's simply no comparison, he wrote, between the impact of an investigation on a suspect and the impact on a victim's family.
A suspect faces the stigma of being charged, convicted and the potential loss of their liberty, he said.

"While no doubt deeply felt on a subjective level, the interest for which (victims and their families) seek compensation do not ordinarily attract legal protection," said Sharpe, writing on behalf of justices Michael Moldaver and Robert Armstrong.

In their lawsuit claiming $2 million in general and punitive damages against the SIU, Simone Wellington and her daughter, Alexis Wellington-Watt, allege the agency's failure to conduct a competent investigation deprived them of their right to have a reasonable understanding of the circumstances surrounding Duane's death.
It also compounded their grief, compromised their participation in a coroner's inquest and reduced their opportunity to recover damages through a civil action.
Refusing to recognize a right to sue the SIU doesn't mean that victims and their families have no other legal recourse, the court was careful to note in its decision.
Victims can apply for compensation from the Criminal Injuries Compensation Board and they can seek to participate in coroners' inquests and apply to be reimbursed for their legal costs, Sharpe said.
They can also express their views through victim impact statements at criminal trials and bring civil actions for damages against police.
"In this country it appears that justice and the legal system are two different things," a disappointed Wellington said Friday night.
Suing the SIU was a last resort after running into roadblocks in other attempts to get answers about her son's death, she said.
Investigators tried to block a lawsuit by the family by arguing that an inquest into Duane's death would answer their questions, she said.
Then they tried to restrict the family's participation in the inquest, Wellington added.
"Kudos to them for their imagination, but I'm not having it," she told the Star .
Wellington said she will instruct her lawyer, Peter Rosenthal, to seek permission to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada.
She and her daughter have launched a civil lawsuit against the two officers involved in Duane's shooting.
